import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components'

[oauth2-proxy](https://oauth2-proxy.github.io/oauth2-proxy/) is a reverse proxy that signs users in
with OIDC before passing requests on. Use it for an app that has no OIDC support of its own, such as an
internal tool: the app needs no code change, and receives the user in request headers.

**Why oauth2-proxy.** The guide needed a proxy that works with any HTTP app, on its own or alongside
whichever web server you already run. oauth2-proxy has a generic
[OIDC provider](https://oauth2-proxy.github.io/oauth2-proxy/configuration/providers/openid_connect), and
[documented options](https://oauth2-proxy.github.io/oauth2-proxy/configuration/overview/) for the two
things this provider asks of a client: `S256` PKCE (`code_challenge_method`) and a private CA
(`provider_ca_files`). Other proxies were not compared by running them.

<Aside type="note" title="What this was tested against">
  oauth2-proxy 7.15.5 (`quay.io/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy:v7.15.5`), running as the proxy itself, against
  released `seamless-auth-api` v0.22.0 and `seamless-auth-oidc-provider` v0.3.0, on 2026-11-04. Nothing
  here needs API v0.23.0. See [What was and was not tested](#what-was-and-was-not-tested): this is a
  local test, not production verification.
</Aside>

---

## 1. Register The Client

The `--help` of oauth2-proxy 7.15.5 shows client secret options and none for `private_key_jwt`, so this
needs
[`allow_client_secrets`](/build/openid-provider-connect-an-app#register-the-client) and an edge restart.

`POST /admin/applications`:

```json
{
  "name": "oauth2-proxy",
  "clientType": "confidential",
  "firstParty": true,
  "tokenEndpointAuthMethod": "client_secret_basic",
  "redirectUris": ["http://127.0.0.1:13003/oauth2/callback"],
  "postLogoutRedirectUris": ["http://127.0.0.1:13003/"],
  "grantTypes": ["authorization_code", "refresh_token"]
}
```

---

## 2. Run It

This is the command that was run. `--network` puts it on the local recipe's compose network, where
`my-upstream` stands for your app. The CA mount is only for a private CA.

```bash
export ISSUER=https://auth.guides.localhost:19443
export CLIENT_ID=...
export CLIENT_SECRET=...

docker run -d --name oauth2-proxy \
  --network provider-guides_default \
  -p 127.0.0.1:13003:4180 \
  -v "$PWD/local/.generated/ca.crt:/etc/oauth2-proxy/seamless-ca.crt:ro" \
  -e OAUTH2_PROXY_HTTP_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0:4180 \
  -e OAUTH2_PROXY_PROVIDER=oidc \
  -e OAUTH2_PROXY_PROVIDER_DISPLAY_NAME=Seamless \
  -e OAUTH2_PROXY_OIDC_ISSUER_URL="$ISSUER" \
  -e OAUTH2_PROXY_CLIENT_ID="$CLIENT_ID" \
  -e OAUTH2_PROXY_CLIENT_SECRET="$CLIENT_SECRET" \
  -e OAUTH2_PROXY_REDIRECT_URL=http://127.0.0.1:13003/oauth2/callback \
  -e OAUTH2_PROXY_UPSTREAMS=http://my-upstream:8080/ \
  -e OAUTH2_PROXY_CODE_CHALLENGE_METHOD=S256 \
  -e 'OAUTH2_PROXY_SCOPE=openid email seamless' \
  -e OAUTH2_PROXY_OIDC_GROUPS_CLAIM=roles \
  -e OAUTH2_PROXY_ALLOWED_GROUPS=user \
  -e 'OAUTH2_PROXY_EMAIL_DOMAINS=*' \
  -e OAUTH2_PROXY_INSECURE_OIDC_SKIP_NONCE=false \
  -e OAUTH2_PROXY_COOKIE_SECRET="$(openssl rand -hex 16)" \
  -e OAUTH2_PROXY_COOKIE_SECURE=false \
  -e OAUTH2_PROXY_SKIP_PROVIDER_BUTTON=true \
  -e OAUTH2_PROXY_WHITELIST_DOMAINS=auth.guides.localhost:19443 \
  -e OAUTH2_PROXY_PROVIDER_CA_FILES=/etc/oauth2-proxy/seamless-ca.crt \
  quay.io/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy:v7.15.5
```

### What each setting does

| Setting                                | Value                     | Why                                                                                                                                  |
| -------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `CODE_CHALLENGE_METHOD`                | `S256`                    | Off by default, and the provider refuses a request without PKCE.                                                                     |
| `SCOPE`                                | `openid email seamless`   | `seamless` adds the `roles` claim. oauth2-proxy's default scopes also worked, because the provider ignores `profile`, but give no roles. |
| `OIDC_GROUPS_CLAIM`, `ALLOWED_GROUPS`  | `roles`, your role        | The provider has no `groups` claim, so read `roles` as groups. A user without the role gets `403` after signing in.                  |
| `EMAIL_DOMAINS`                        | `*`, or your domain       | `*` lets any signed-in user through this check, so restrict by role or domain.                                             |
| `INSECURE_OIDC_SKIP_NONCE`             | `false`                   | Its default is `true`. The provider returned the nonce, so verification passes.                                                      |
| `COOKIE_SECRET`                        | 32 random characters      | Encrypts oauth2-proxy's session cookie.                                      |
| `COOKIE_SECURE`                        | `false` on loopback only  | Needed for plain `http` here. **Remove it in a deployment**: the default is `true`.                                                  |
| `WHITELIST_DOMAINS`                    | The issuer's host and port | Allows the sign-out redirect to the issuer.                                                                                         |
| `PROVIDER_CA_FILES`                    | The CA path               | Private CA only.                                                                                                                     |

The environment names follow oauth2-proxy's
[flag to environment variable rule](https://oauth2-proxy.github.io/oauth2-proxy/configuration/overview/).

### For your deployment

Replace the issuer, redirect URL and whitelist with your own `https` values, remove
`OAUTH2_PROXY_COOKIE_SECURE`, and with a publicly trusted certificate remove the CA mount and
`PROVIDER_CA_FILES`. Those values were not run.

**Make the app reachable only through the proxy.** It trusts the headers below, so anyone who can reach
it directly can send their own.

---

## 3. What The App Receives

The test's upstream printed these headers:

| Header               | Value                                                                       |
| -------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `X-Forwarded-User`   | The `sub`, the Seamless user ID. There is no username claim to use instead. |
| `X-Forwarded-Email`  | The `email` claim                                                           |
| `X-Forwarded-Groups` | The `roles` claim, with the settings above. Absent otherwise.               |

---

## 4. Check It

1. Open `http://127.0.0.1:13003/`. A request with no session gets a `302`, and the browser goes to the
   hosted page.
2. Sign in. A first-party client shows no consent page.
3. The app's response shows the headers above.

---

## 5. Sign Out

oauth2-proxy's `/oauth2/sign_out` clears its own cookie and follows `rd`. To end the Seamless session as
well, set `rd` to the provider's end session URL. Each level is URL encoded:

```text
/oauth2/sign_out?rd=<encoded: <issuer>/session/end?client_id=<id>&post_logout_redirect_uri=<encoded: http://127.0.0.1:13003/>>
```

In Python:

```python
import urllib.parse as u
inner = u.quote('http://127.0.0.1:13003/', safe='')
print('/oauth2/sign_out?rd=' + u.quote(f'{issuer}/session/end?client_id={client_id}&post_logout_redirect_uri={inner}', safe=''))
```

The hosted page asks whether to sign out of everything or only this app. After **Sign out**, the browser
returns to the app, whose request has no session, so it lands on the hosted sign-in page.

---

## Troubleshooting

Each of these was hit while testing.

| What you see                                                                                                                                          | Cause and fix                                                                     |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The container exits at startup: `error while discovery OIDC configuration ... tls: failed to verify certificate`                                      | It does not trust the issuer's CA. Set `PROVIDER_CA_FILES`.                       |
| At startup, `Warning: Your provider supports PKCE methods ["S256"], but you have not enabled one with --code-challenge-method`, then an error page on sign-in | Set `CODE_CHALLENGE_METHOD=S256`.                                       |
| `403 Forbidden` on `/oauth2/callback`, after the hosted page                                                                                          | The user's roles do not include `ALLOWED_GROUPS`. This is the check working.      |
| `X-Forwarded-Groups` is missing                                                                                                                       | `OIDC_GROUPS_CLAIM=roles` and the `seamless` scope are both needed.               |

Registration and shared-secret errors are in the
[generic guide](/build/openid-provider-connect-an-app#troubleshooting).

---

## What Was And Was Not Tested

**Tested.** The command above, in front of a small upstream that printed its request headers, with
Playwright's Chromium and a virtual WebAuthn authenticator: a new user registering, a passkey sign-in
from a clean browser, the headers reaching the upstream, sign-out, and a `403` for a user lacking the
allowed role. The stack was the local recipe from
[seamless-auth-oidc-provider](https://github.com/fells-code/seamless-auth-oidc-provider/tree/main/local), adjusted as described in the
[generic guide](/build/openid-provider-connect-an-app#what-was-and-was-not-tested).

**Not tested.** A browser that trusts the CA normally, a real authenticator, `https` or
`COOKIE_SECURE=true`, a production deployment, oauth2-proxy behind nginx, Traefik or Caddy
(`auth_request` or forward-auth mode), session refresh (`--cookie-refresh`), Redis session storage, or
any other reverse proxy.
